body:
Digital access requires skills as well as connectivity

An internet connection is useful only when a person can operate the required device and understand the information presented. Digital inclusion therefore involves more than constructing a communications network. Two important initiatives illustrate different methods of addressing these needs: PMGDISHA focused on basic digital skills, while BHASHINI provides language technologies for accessing digital information and services.

PMGDISHA: Basic digital literacy for rural residents

Pradhan Mantri Gramin Digital Saksharta Abhiyan (PMGDISHA) was approved in February 2017 under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. Its objective was to make eligible rural residents digitally literate so they could use digital devices and internet-based services.

The scheme targeted 6 crore rural households, with the aim of training 1 eligible person per household. Its target group consisted of digitally illiterate people in rural areas, generally in the 14–60 years age group, from households with no digitally literate member.

Implementation used the network of Common Service Centres (CSCs) and was carried out through CSC e-Governance Services India Limited. The training covered basic use of computers, smartphones and other digital devices, internet browsing, electronic communication, access to citizen services and digital financial transactions.

The programme provided 20 hours of training across 5 learning modules: introduction to digital devices, operating digital devices, introduction to the internet, communication using the internet and applications of the internet. Training and certification were distinct stages; completing training was not automatically the same as obtaining certification.

PMGDISHA is no longer an ongoing enrolment scheme

PMGDISHA concluded on 31 March 2024. Official reporting stated that approximately 6.39 crore individuals were trained by the scheme's conclusion, compared with the target of 6 crore. These are historical scheme achievements, not evidence that fresh enrolment continued in November 2026.

BHASHINI: Multilingual digital services

BHASHINI is an artificial-intelligence-based language technology initiative launched in July 2022 under the National Language Translation Mission. It aims to reduce language barriers when people use digital information and services.

Its responsible organisation is the Digital India BHASHINI Division (DIBD) under the Digital India Corporation (DIC), MeitY. BHASHINI brings together language datasets, AI models and technological services that government departments, developers and institutions can integrate into applications.

Important functions include machine translation, which converts text between languages; speech-to-text, which converts spoken language into text; and text-to-speech, which converts text into spoken output. These functions can make digital services easier to use in Indian languages.

For example, a Gujarati-speaking citizen may understand a public-service explanation more easily when it is available in Gujarati rather than only in English. BHASHINI provides language technology that can support such an interface. It does not itself decide the citizen's eligibility for a government service.

A Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology release dated 4 November 2026 reported support for 36 Indian text languages, 23 Indian voice languages and 35 international languages. These are different capability categories. They must not be read as a claim that every language is supported identically for every text and speech function.

In Gujarat, a July 2026 agreement between DIBD and the Knowledge Consortium of Gujarat concerned exploration of multilingual AI applications in education and public services. An agreement to develop or explore applications should not be confused with confirmation that every proposed application has already been deployed.

Comparison and current status

AttributePMGDISHABHASHINI
Main need addressedDigital literacyLanguage accessibility
Start2017July 2022
Responsible organisationsMeitY and CSC implementation networkDIBD, DIC and MeitY
Primary usersEligible rural learnersCitizens and organisations using multilingual services
Main benefitBasic digital skills trainingTranslation and speech technologies
Status at cutoffConcluded on 31 March 2024Operating in November 2026

The core distinction is learning to use technology versus being able to use technology in a familiar language. Digital literacy and language access can reinforce each other, but they are not interchangeable.

Prelims focus

  • PMGDISHA was approved in February 2017.
  • PMGDISHA targeted 6 crore rural households, with 1 eligible trainee per household.
  • Its stated trainee age group was 14–60 years.
  • PMGDISHA concluded on 31 March 2024.
  • BHASHINI launched in July 2022 and operates through DIBD under DIC, MeitY.
  • Trap: PMGDISHA is a completed training scheme; BHASHINI is an operating language-technology platform.

[Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, Press Information Bureau, 'Objective of PMGDISHA', 30 March 2022, eligibility and objectives; Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, Press Information Bureau, parliamentary reply on PMGDISHA training and certification, July 2024, training modules and results; Press Information Bureau, 'Digital India Program Has Enabled Wider Access to Digital Services and Opportunities', 18 March 2026, PMGDISHA conclusion; Press Information Bureau, 'Year End Review 2022: MeitY', BHASHINI launch; Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, Press Information Bureau, 'Digital India BHASHINI Division and SEBI Sign MoU', 4 November 2026, platform capabilities; official online sources consulted 14 November 2026.]

title: PMGDISHA and BHASHINI: Digital Literacy Versus Language Access

body:
What Aadhaar provides

Aadhaar is a unique identity number issued to eligible individuals through India's Aadhaar identity system. It is a 12-digit number and is designed to support reliable identification and authentication.

The responsible authority is the Unique Identification Authority of India (UIDAI), a statutory authority under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. Its statutory basis is the Aadhaar (Targeted Delivery of Financial and Other Subsidies, Benefits and Services) Act, 2016.

UIDAI's enrolment system uses specified demographic and biometric information to establish a person's identity and reduce the risk of issuing multiple Aadhaar numbers to the same person. Demographic information includes identifying personal details, while biometric information may include fingerprints, iris scans and a photograph, subject to the applicable enrolment procedure.

Who may enrol?

Under Section 2(v) of the Aadhaar Act, a resident is generally an individual who has lived in India for a total of 182 days or more during the 12 months immediately preceding the enrolment application. Eligible residents may seek enrolment with the required supporting information and documents.

There is also a separate enrolment provision for Non-Resident Indians holding valid Indian passports, who need not satisfy that 182-day waiting period for Aadhaar enrolment. Thus, the ordinary residence rule should not be stated as an exceptionless condition applying to every permitted category of applicant.

Aadhaar is not restricted to adults. Children may also be enrolled with the consent of a parent or guardian; below age 5, only their photograph is captured, with mandatory biometric updates at ages 5 and 15.

Identification and authentication are not the same

Identification concerns establishing which individual a record refers to. Authentication concerns verifying that identity through an authorised process, using permitted identifying information or credentials. Aadhaar provides an identity infrastructure that can support authentication for participating services.

For example, a department may use Aadhaar-based authentication, where lawful and applicable, to verify an applicant's identity. The department must still determine whether the applicant meets the separate eligibility conditions for the requested service or benefit. Authentication does not itself approve the application.

Aadhaar does not prove citizenship

Section 9 of the Aadhaar Act, 2016 states that an Aadhaar number or its authentication does not, by itself, confer or prove citizenship or domicile. Aadhaar is an identity system, not a citizenship certificate.

Aadhaar compared with other digital systems

  • Aadhaar: provides a unique identity number and supports identity verification.
  • DigiLocker: makes digitally issued documents accessible and shareable.
  • UMANG: provides access to participating government services.
  • UPI: enables digital payments through participating accounts and applications.
  • AePS: uses Aadhaar authentication in specified banking transactions when the necessary account and system conditions are satisfied.

These systems may interact, but they have different functions. Possessing an Aadhaar number does not automatically create a bank account, establish entitlement to a subsidy or authorise a payment.

Status at the 14 November 2026 cutoff: Aadhaar and UIDAI remained operational. The Aadhaar Act and applicable UIDAI enrolment rules determine the legal conditions for its use.

Prelims focus

  • Aadhaar is a 12-digit identity number.
  • UIDAI is the statutory authority under MeitY.
  • The principal legislation is the Aadhaar Act, 2016.
  • Section 2(v): ordinary resident criterion of 182 days in the preceding 12 months.
  • Section 9: Aadhaar does not by itself prove citizenship or domicile.
  • Trap: Aadhaar authentication is not the same as approval of a government benefit.

[Unique Identification Authority of India, 'The Aadhaar Act, 2016', Sections 2(v), 3 and 9; UIDAI, 'About UIDAI', statutory authority and ministry; UIDAI, 'Enrolment and Update', resident and Non-Resident Indian enrolment provisions; official online sources consulted 14 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Aadhaar authentication verifies identity; the department separately checks benefit eligibility. Aadhaar alone does not prove citizenship or domicile.
pictures.caption: Aadhaar can verify identity, but identity verification and benefit eligibility remain separate decisions.

title: Aadhaar: Digital Identity, Authentication and Eligibility

body:
DigiLocker: An electronic document system

DigiLocker is a digital document platform under the Digital India programme. Launched in 2015, it enables users to access, store, share and verify electronic documents. It operates through the National e-Governance Division (NeGD), Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology.

Its purpose is to reduce dependence on paper documents by connecting the person who needs a document with the organisation that originally issued it. A board of education may issue a digital marksheet, for example, which an eligible student can access through DigiLocker and share with an institution that needs to verify it.

The DigiLocker ecosystem includes distinct roles:

  • Issuer: an authorised organisation that creates or makes an authentic digital document available, such as an educational board or government department.
  • Holder: the individual entitled to access the document.
  • Requester or verifier: an authorised organisation that seeks to receive or verify a document for a legitimate purpose, subject to the applicable process.

Issued Documents and Uploaded Documents

DigiLocker distinguishes between documents supplied directly through an authorised issuer and files a user uploads personally.

Document categoryOriginImportant distinction
Issued DocumentsParticipating authorised issuerCan be authenticated against the issuer's digital record
Uploaded DocumentsUser's own uploaded fileUploading alone does not establish that an issuer authenticated the document

Under Rule 9A of the Information Technology (Preservation and Retention of Information by Intermediaries Providing Digital Locker Facilities) Rules, 2016, documents issued or shared through the prescribed DigiLocker arrangement are treated at par with corresponding original physical documents. This legal equivalence must not be interpreted to mean that any unverified photograph or scan uploaded by a user automatically becomes an officially issued certificate.

DigiLocker stores and provides access to documents; the original issuing authority remains responsible for the document it issues.

UMANG: A unified service interface

UMANG stands for Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance. It was publicly launched on 23 November 2017 and was developed under MeitY and NeGD.

UMANG provides a unified interface through which citizens can access participating services from Union, state and local government organisations. A user does not necessarily need to locate a different application for every participating service.

Depending on the department and service, UMANG can allow users to obtain information, submit requests or access government-related facilities. However, UMANG is generally the access platform; the government department responsible for a service continues to decide the application according to that service's rules.

For example, a student may retrieve a digitally issued marksheet through DigiLocker while using UMANG to access a participating government service. If the service needs identity verification, an appropriate identification or authentication mechanism may also be used. These functions are connected but remain distinct.

Scheme-card comparison

AttributeDigiLockerUMANG
CategoryDigital document platformGovernment service platform
Main purposeAccess and share authentic digital documentsAccess participating government services
Responsible organisationsNeGD, MeitYMeitY and NeGD
Introduced20152017
UsersPeople and organisations using digital documentsCitizens using participating public services
Status at cutoffOperatingOperating

Neither platform is a general cash-benefit scheme. Access to a particular document requires the relevant issuer's record, while access to a particular service requires satisfaction of that service's applicable conditions.

Prelims focus

  • DigiLocker: digital documents; launched in 2015.
  • UMANG: unified government-service interface; launched on 23 November 2017.
  • Both are associated with NeGD and MeitY.
  • Rule 9A governs the legal treatment of documents issued through DigiLocker.
  • Trap: A user-uploaded scan is not automatically an officially issued DigiLocker document.
